scenes.narration: Setbacks came early for George W. Bush, and the response to them is the real story. George Walker Bush (born July 6, 1946) is an American former politician, businessman, and U.S. Air Force veteran who served as the 43rd president of the United States from 2001 to 2009.

The legacy of George W. Bush outlived the circumstances that produced it. A member of the Republican Party, he served as the 46th governor of Texas from 1995 to 2000. Born into the prominent Bush family in New Haven, Connecticut, Bush flew warplanes in the Texas Air National Guard in his twenties.

Few lives travel as far as that of George W. Bush, and the distance is the point. After graduating from Harvard Business School in 1975, he worked in the oil industry. He later co-owned the Major League Baseball team Texas Rangers before being elected governor of Texas in 1994.

The childhood of George W. Bush contains the adult in small print. As governor, Bush successfully sponsored legislation for tort reform, increased education funding, set higher standards for schools, and reformed the criminal justice system. In the 2000 presidential election, he defeated Democratic incumbent vice president Al Gore while losing the popular vote after a narrow and contested United States Electoral College win, which involved the Supreme Court decision Bush v.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of George W. Bush — in that order. In his first term, Bush signed a major tax-cut program and an education-reform bill, the No Child Left Behind Act. He pushed for socially conservative efforts such as the Partial-Birth Abortion Ban Act, restrictions on same-sex marriage, and faith-based initiatives.

The turning point in the life of George W. Bush looked like a failure at the time. He also initiated the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, in 2003, to address the global AIDS epidemic. The September 11 attacks during 2001 decisively reshaped his administration, resulting in the start of the war on terror and the creation of the Department of Homeland Security.

Every biography of George W. Bush has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Bush ordered the invasion of Afghanistan in an effort to overthrow the Taliban, destroy al-Qaeda, and capture Osama bin Laden. He also ordered the 2003 invasion of Iraq to overthrow Saddam Hussein's regime, citing claims that it possessed weapons of mass destruction and had ties with al-Qaeda.

The education of George W. Bush happened mostly outside any school. Bush later signed the Medicare Modernization Act, which created Medicare Part D. Bush was re-elected in 2004, winning the popular vote against Democratic nominee John Kerry.

What George W. Bush wanted at the start and what George W. Bush got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. During his second term, Bush negotiated various free trade agreements, appointed John Roberts and Samuel Alito to the Supreme Court, and sought major changes to Social Security and immigration laws, both of which ultimately failed in Congress. He was widely criticized for his administration's handling of Hurricane Katrina and revelations of torture against detainees at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq.

The defining trait of George W. Bush was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Amid his unpopularity, the Democrats regained control of Congress in the 2006 elections. As his presidency came to a close, the country experienced a financial crisis, resulting in the Great Recession, prompting his administration and Congress to push through emergency economic measures aimed at stabilizing the financial system, including the Troubled Asset Relief Program.

Those who met George W. Bush at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. After his second term, Bush returned to Texas, where he has maintained a low public profile. At various points in his presidency, he was both among the most popular and among the least popular presidents in U.S. history.

The private years of George W. Bush explain the public decades better than any speech. He received the highest recorded approval ratings in the wake of the September 11 attacks, and one of the lowest ratings during the 2008 financial crisis. Bush left office as one of the most unpopular U.S. presidents; however, public opinion of him has improved in his post-presidency.

The family George W. Bush came from matters more than the legends admit. George Walker Bush was born on July 6, 1946, at Grace-New Haven Hospital in New Haven, Connecticut. He is the first child of George Herbert Walker Bush and Barbara Pierce, and was raised in Midland and Houston, Texas.

The first real success of George W. Bush arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. His father was Ronald Reagan's vice president from 1981 to 1989 and the 41st president of the United States from 1989 to 1993. Bush has distant English and German ancestry, along with more distant (over seven generations removed) Dutch, Welsh, Irish, French, and Scottish roots.

The last chapter of George W. Bush was written long after the fame. Bush attended public schools in Midland, Texas, until the family moved to Houston after he had completed seventh grade. He then spent two years at The Kinkaid School, a college-preparatory school in Piney Point Village, Texas.

The whole life of George W. Bush reads like a single decision repeated. Bush later attended Phillips Academy, a boarding school in Andover, Massachusetts, where he played baseball and was the head cheerleader during his senior year. He attended Yale University from 1964 to 1968, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in history.

Between the birth and the legend of George W. Bush lie the years that actually decide it. During this time, he was a cheerleader and a member of the Delta Kappa Epsilon, serving as the president of the fraternity during his senior year. Bush became a member of the Skull and Bones society as a senior.

The reputation of George W. Bush was built in the middle, not at the edges. Bush was a rugby union player and was on Yale's 1st XV. His grade point average during his first three years at Yale was 77, and he had a similar average under a nonnumerical rating system in his final year.

Somebody like George W. Bush should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. In May 1968, Bush joined the United States Air Force and was commissioned into the Texas Air National Guard. After two years of training in active-duty service, he was assigned to Houston, flying Convair F-102s with the 147th Reconnaissance Wing out of Ellington Field Joint Reserve Base.

The life of George W. Bush begins far from where the story usually starts. In June 2005, the Department of Defense released all the records of Bush's Texas Air National Guard service, which remain in its official archives. In late 1972 and early 1973, he drilled with the 187th Fighter Wing of the Alabama Air National Guard.

George W. Bush was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. In 1972, Bush was suspended from flying for failure to take a scheduled physical exam. In 1977, Bush established Arbusto Energy, a small oil exploration company, which began operations in 1978.

To understand where George W. Bush ended up, start with where George W. Bush began. In 1984, his company merged with the larger Spectrum 7, and Bush became chairman. The company was hurt by decreased oil prices, and it folded into Harken Energy Corporation, with Bush becoming a member of Harken's board of directors.

The road from the beginning to the peak of George W. Bush ran through years nobody filmed. Questions of possible insider trading involving Harken arose, but a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation concluded that the information Bush had at the time of his stock sale was not sufficient to constitute insider trading. In April 1989, Bush arranged for a group of investors to purchase a controlling interest in Major League Baseball's Texas Rangers for $89 million and invested $500,000 himself to start.

Each stage of the life of George W. Bush made the next stage possible. He actively led the team's projects and regularly attended its games, often choosing to sit in the open stands with fans. Bush's sale of his shares in the Rangers in 1998 brought him over $15 million from his initial $800,000 investment.

The people who knew George W. Bush young describe someone already restless. In the early or mid 1990s, before his gubernatorial campaign, Bush briefly considered running for Commissioner of Baseball. Bush's opponent, Kent Hance, portrayed him as out of touch with rural Texans, and Bush lost the election, receiving 46.8 percent of the vote to Hance's 53.2 percent.

What George W. Bush built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Bush and his family moved to Washington, D.C., in 1988 to work on his father's campaign for the U.S. presidency. He was a campaign advisor and liaison to the media, and assisted his father by campaigning across the country.

By the time George W. Bush reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. The rise of George W. Bush was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Bush declared his candidacy for the 1994 Texas gubernatorial election at the same time his brother Jeb sought the governorship in Florida. After easily winning the Republican primary, Bush faced popular Democratic incumbent governor Ann Richards.

Setbacks came early for George W. Bush, and the response to them is the real story. In the course of the campaign, Bush pledged to sign a bill allowing Texans to obtain permits to carry concealed weapons. Richards had vetoed the bill, but Bush signed it into law after he became governor.

The legacy of George W. Bush outlived the circumstances that produced it. The Atlantic, and others, connected the lesbian rumor to Karl Rove, but Rove denied being involved. Bush won the general election with 53.5 percent of the vote against Richards' 45.9 percent.

Few lives travel as far as that of George W. Bush, and the distance is the point. Bush used a budget surplus to push through Texas's largest tax cut, $2 billion. He extended government funding for organizations providing education on the dangers of alcohol and drug use and abuse, and helping to reduce domestic violence.

Bush presided over 152 executions, more than any previous governor in modern American history; critics such as Helen Prejean argue that he failed to give serious consideration to clemency requests.

Supporters pointed to his efforts to raise the salaries of teachers and improve educational test scores.
